top_choice_rationale: P001 (Autor, Hanson, Dorn, B022) asks a first-order question about who bears the cost of trade and technology shocks, and it uses transparent designs that have been replicated, re-analysed and contested for about a decade. The contested parts are the size and persistence of the effects, not whether adjustment is slow and costly. Autor, Dorn and Hanson jointly authored the central China-shock papers, so credit for the evidence named in a citation limited to empirical analyses is clean. The citation should not claim the task-model theory, whose originators lie outside the credited set. P002 (Melitz and Helpman, B012) is a close second. It has a very mature, stable core mechanism and clean two-name credit. I weigh it slightly lower because Bernard-Jensen and Eaton-Kortum have unaddressed claims, and its welfare magnitudes depend on functional form. Both proposals are clearly preferable to no award.
recusal_note: No tie to Autor, Hanson, Dorn, Helpman or Melitz is apparent from my profile. My research on capital-skill complementarity and technology and inequality is adjacent to B022. I treat that as subject expertise, not merit. My long-term co-authors, including Timo Boppart and John Hassler, who support P002, are not credited names on either proposal. Disclosed, not adjudicated.
